absaetze.t: Ce jeudi 12 novembre, les forces de l’ordre ont arrêté sept personnes présentes lors des blocus lycéens. Un rassemblement a eu lieu à 12h30 devant le commissariat de police, pour soutenir les interpellés, dont Lisa, une des figures du Poing Levé à Strasbourg.
Cet article est en accès libre. Pour soutenir Rue89 Strasbourg, abonnez-vous.
Publié le 12 novembre 2026 ·
Imprimé le 12 novembre 2026 à 21h19 ·
Modifié le 12 novembre 2026 ·
2 minutes

« On est ici pour exiger la libération de Lisa et des autres étudiants et lycéens », lance une militante du Poing levé, devant le commissariat de Strasbourg. Ce jeudi 12 novembre, à 12h30, une petite centaine de personnes se sont rassemblées en soutien aux sept personnes interpellées lors des blocus lycéens le même jour.

Depuis plusieurs semaines, les étudiants rejoignent les lycéens lors des blocus. « C’est eux qui ont initié le mouvement, c’est important de continuer à les soutenir et d’être avec eux face à la répression, pour qu’il y ait la présence d’adultes », lance Désiré devant le commissariat. Présent le matin même devant le lycée Marie-Curie, l’étudiant en droit témoigne de la stratégie des forces de l’ordre :
« Il y a une volonté de séparer les étudiants des lycéens et de cibler certaines personnes, notamment celles qui avaient des mégaphones en main. »

Parmi les sept personnes arrêtées ce jeudi matin, on retrouve Lisa, une figure du Poing levé, qui filme les blocus lycéens en direct sur TikTok. Depuis quelques semaines, la militante est présente sur les réseaux sociaux, à visage découvert, pour « dénoncer la répression et les violences policières », explique Lou, militante à Révolution permanente et présente lors de l’arrestation de Lisa :
« Lorsque je l’ai rejointe devant le lycée Marie-Curie, elle m’a dit qu’elle était visée par les forces de l’ordre aujourd’hui, qu’ils l’avaient pointée du doigt à plusieurs reprises. »
Arrestation par deux policiers en civil

Devant cet établissement vers 8h15, un affrontement à base de pétards et de gaz lacrymogènes a éclaté entre quelques jeunes et les forces de l’ordre. L’attroupement s’est ensuite dispersé et Lisa et ses camarades se sont réfugiés dans le campus universitaire. « Il y avait aussi des policiers à moto et en civil sur le campus. Lisa s’est dite suivie par deux hommes en civil avant de rejoindre [un groupe de manifestants] ». Les étudiants se sont ensuite à nouveau dispersés, peu avant 9h30 :

« On est sortis du campus et on a tourné une vidéo en filmant Lisa pour faire un bilan de ce qui s’est passé ce matin. On a vu deux gendarmes nous observer au loin, puis une voiture banalisée s’est garée et deux policiers en civil sont sortis et ont interpellé Lisa. »

Pour beaucoup de militants, cette arrestation est symbolique. « Ce qui les énerve, c’est qu’il y ait des témoins de cette répression du mouvement lycéen », estime Désiré. Au cours du rassemblement, plusieurs militants ont appelé à poursuivre la mobilisation en soutien aux lycéens. « J’invite tous ceux qui ont du temps à se rendre sur les blocus pour les protéger et leur apporter du matériel comme des masques ou du sérum physiologique », propose Désiré.
Questionnée sur les motifs des interpellations du 12 novembre, la police nationale n’a pas répondu à Rue89 Strasbourg.

items.titel: Putin takes hard line in US talks as Ukraine says Starlink disrupted again
items.anriss: Russian president says he would target any foreign troops sent to Ukraine and refuses to soften territorial demands

absaetze.t: Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops deployed to Ukraine, in a series of hardline remarks that came as the Ukrainian military faced renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service.

During the talks at the Kremlin with the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Thursday, the Russian president refused to soften his territorial demands, insisting on full control over four Ukrainian regions that Moscow claims to have annexed.
He also ruled out accepting the deployment of foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine, describing such a move as a “continuation of war”.

Putin’s comments appeared to severely dampen hopes that a peace deal could be within reach, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there was a “window of opportunity” to reach an agreement before the end of 2026.

The latest trip to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, who have made numerous visits to Russia, was partly aimed at securing European participation in future negotiations, according to two people familiar with the talks.

Speaking after the meeting, Witkoff confirmed that European representatives would join the next round of talks. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he told reporters as he boarded a plane leaving Moscow.
The US envoys will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet Zelenskyy and debrief him on the Moscow meeting.

Amid a flurry of diplomatic activity, including the recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin appears to have succeeded in reframing negotiations over the war in Ukraine as part of a broader discussion about European security.
But Europe is wary of Russian attempts to focus discussions on a European security architecture, while Moscow continues to pound Ukraine with bombs and missiles.

The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told reporters: “We already have a European security architecture in place.” Kallas pointed to the cold war-era Helsinki accords and the Budapest memorandum, which guaranteed the territorial integrity of Ukraine. “The problem is that Russia is not keeping to those agreements, so right now the focus should be that Russia actually keeps to their obligations … and they don’t attack another country again.” Focusing on a European security architecture was a “distraction” without a ceasefire, she added.
Both Washington and Moscow have been urging European leaders to appoint a single representative to lead negotiations on their behalf.
“Once a representative is appointed, a chief negotiator authorised to speak on Europe’s behalf, there will be a four-way dialogue,” Putin said on Thursday.

EU leaders are due to discuss the issue of who speaks for Europe on Friday, but so far have declined to nominate one person to speak for the bloc. One EU official said the EU would be represented by its institutions when issues concerning the union were on the table, but played down any imminent appointment. They said: “Do I expect an agreement on a special representative? My answer is no, I don’t.”
Kallas suggested she – as the EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy – should represent the EU in talks, alongside António Costa, the president of the European Council.

More than 45 European leaders are meeting in Dublin for the European Political Community summit, a gathering that brings together nearly every country on the continent, apart from the leaders of Belarus and Russia.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, played down the importance of having a single European negotiator, saying “the content determines the format”. “There is no more US support. So there [are] some mediations, fine,” he said, referring to the process led by Kushner and Witkoff. “But at the end of the day we will be the one to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said it was first necessary to get Putin to the negotiating table before deciding on a European envoy. Merz said: “It’s not about individuals. What matters is that Putin is prepared to hold talks.”

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy accused Musk’s Starlink satellite service of damaging Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian drone attacks, after Ukrainian military officials reported new restrictions on the system.

According to Zelenskyy, Starshield, a military version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, has for several days been subject to speed limits of 100mph (161km/h) along the frontline and in Russian-occupied territory.
Similar restrictions last month prompted confusion over who had ordered them, with Musk and the Trump administration pointing fingers at each other before the service was partly restored.

The latest restrictions had made it harder for Ukrainian forces to intercept Russia’s increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy said, accusing the service of “helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine”.
Kyiv has contacted Washington to seek an explanation for the disruption, which Zelenskyy said appeared to be deliberate rather than a technical fault.

items.titel: ‘Win-win’ deal with EU could be done, Andy Burnham says
items.anriss: Prime minister says reset could be a deal ‘like the Brexit people thought they were voting for in 2016’

absaetze.t: Andy Burnham has said he believes a “win-win” deal could be done with the EU that could be “more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016”.

The prime minister was meeting fellow leaders at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, ahead of a keenly anticipated EU-UK summit next week, where he hopes to bring Britain closer to Europe.

At the bilateral summit the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, but the question of tuition fees for European students remains a stumbling block.
Burnham said: “I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe.
“The deal is not done, and there’ll be some long nights ahead in the next seven days.”
He said the reset would be about whether we can “take a step back to closer working relationships with Europe”.
Burnham added: “We ended up with a far harder Brexit, I think, than people thought they were getting when they went to the polls.”
The EU has said the prized food and drink deal and emissions-trading agreement may not enter into force without a deal on tuition fees in which European students would pay domestic rates.

Burnham said it was a package deal, but would not be drawn on whether he accepted the link. “I’m going to be fighting hard for these benefits for Britain in the next seven days … they will make a real difference. If I can do anything to address the cost of living crisis, I should be doing it.”
He has previously said the food and drink deal, which will ease Brexit red tape, will add 0.4% to British GDP.

The prime minister also said David Cameron had been wrong to argue that Britain’s problems had “nothing to do with Brexit”, adding there would be “long nights ahead” to negotiate a reset with the EU before the summit.

Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum, told Bloomberg News that Burnham should not seek to bring Britain back into the EU, arguing that the UK’s problems had nothing to do with its exit from the EU.

Asked about those remarks, Burnham said: “I think he is wrong to say that the low growth that we’ve had over the last decade has, quote, ‘nothing to do with Brexit’. I would say the evidence says otherwise.
“It feels like his intervention is more about unity in the Conservative party than it is about fighting for the British interests.”

Burnham has recently said he is open to rejoining the single market, customs union or to “go all the way” by rejoining the EU. He said a deeper relationship would be the outcome of future talks “and it will be in the outcome of that negotiation that then we will take a decision as a cabinet, on what, if anything, comes next”.
Earlier on Thursday, the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said she wanted to see Britain rejoin the EU, but warned that negotiations would not be easy after the “trauma” of the Brexit years.

She said: “I would very much like to see Britain back in Europe, but, of course, we also have in the European Union, a lot of, I would say, trauma from Britain leaving, so the negotiations will not be that easy.”
Burnham is expected to make the EU reset the centrepiece of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet on Monday night – though it will range widely across foreign policy challenges.

No 10 sources said the speech would be focused on the upcoming Brussels summit – and look ahead to the next stage in 2027 – rather than outline what a more permanent close relationship might look like.
Officials at the UK-EU summit will also discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, expected to focus on a joint migration pact.
It could also target collaboration on law enforcement and borders, visas for touring artists, and mutual recognition of qualifications.

Ministry of Justice officials are also trying to water down an EU ultimatum on halting the deportation of foreign national offenders. “This is the classic wheeze that the EU always pulls at the last minute of negotiations,” one Whitehall source said.

The next week is expected to be fraught with last-minute negotiations. Key will be access to Made in Europe, which has the potential to lock British firms out of continental supply chains and public contracts if no deal is done.
Negotiations could be challenging despite the lure of the UK making a potential concession on tuition fees in exchange for inclusion in the Made in Europe legislation.
The EU has long said there cannot be a deal on Made in Europe at the summit, because it has yet to finalise its own position.
The joint communique for 2027 is expected to call for strengthening efforts between the UK and the most exposed member states to the small boats crisis in the Channel.
This will centre on both the EU’s Channel action plan, already in place since June this year, and a possible framework for a wider bespoke EU-UK migration plan.

The UK is believed to be pushing for access to the Eurodac database, which carries the fingerprints of asylum seekers, as well as to the Schengen Information System (SIS), which records details on fugitives, missing people and stolen goods.
The UK was the third biggest user of SIS before it lost access through Brexit.

items.titel: EU Parliament asked to lift immunity of German far-right MEP accused of baseball‑bat attack on teen
items.anriss: The European Parliament has received a request to waive the immunity of a German far-right MEP to allow his prosecution for allegedly drink-driving and violently assaulting a minor with a baseball bat.

absaetze.t: The European Parliament has received a request to waive the immunity of a German far-right MEP to allow his prosecution for allegedly drink-driving and violently assaulting a minor with a baseball bat.

Parliament president Roberta Metsola confirmed having received a request to waive immunity of Arno Bausemer, of the Europe of Sovereign Nations hard-right group who is also the Alternative for Germany treasurer for Saxony-Anhalt, on Wednesday (11 November), so that east German region can prosecute him.
Bausemer is accused of attacking a 14-year-old with a baseball bat during the state’s election campaign in August.
He admitted to having “caught the teenager red-handed”, who he said was vandalising AfD campaign posters, and that he used a baseball bat.
“A suspected blunt weapon was allegedly used,” the Saxony-Anhalt State Criminal Police Office (LKA) confirmed.
A few days later, the MEP was stopped at a traffic control, where a blood sample reportedly showed an alcohol level of one gram per litre – double the allowed limit in Germany.

Parliamentary immunity is in place so that MEPs can “truly perform their mandate independently,” without fear of unjustified legal action, Wouter Wolfs, politics researcher at the KU Leuven, told EUobserver.

Parliamentary immunity guarantees MEPs will not be detained because of their opinions or how they voted, but also for offences they may be accused of. It protects politicians from legal battles designed to distract their attention from their parliamentary duties.
The only exception is when they were caught in the act - though what that means is sometimes disputed.
Currently, the immunity of 10 MEPs is under review in the European parliament, for offences ranging from a labour dispute to holocaust denial.

In some recent cases, the parliament kept MEPs immunity on “rather doubtful grounds,” Wolfs said, namely when their political allies protected them, but in essence, MEPs most often end up being put on trial.

The trouble with the immunity provision, German Green MEP Daniel Freund told EUobserver, is that it takes a long time to actually waive it, “undermining both parliament’s credibility and the principle that everyone is equal before the law.”

In most cases, the time between receiving a complaint by the parliament’s legal affairs committee - tasked with immunity waivers - and a plenary vote deciding on the matter is about five months, but up to a year in some cases.
Wolfs said he would expect the parliament to waive Bausemer’s immunity, so that the proceedings against him in his case may resume.

items.titel: L'agenda européen : les principaux événements prévus du 16 au 22 novembre 2026
items.anriss: Lundi 16 novembre , le premier Forum européen sur l'élargissement réunit à Bruxelles dirigeants et représentants de la société civile. Après une ouverture dimanche, les discussions porteront sur les réformes nécessaires pour accueillir de …

absaetze.t: La diplomatie européenne se mobilise autour de l'Ukraine, tandis que Bruxelles publie ses nouvelles prévisions économiques. Un sommet UE-Royaume-Uni, le vote du budget de la Sécurité sociale au Sénat et la clôture de la COP31 complètent les principaux rendez-vous de la semaine.

Lundi 16 novembre, le premier Forum européen sur l'élargissement réunit à Bruxelles dirigeants et représentants de la société civile. Après une ouverture dimanche, les discussions porteront sur les réformes nécessaires pour accueillir de nouveaux membres, notamment dans les Balkans occidentaux, et préparer l'UE à fonctionner avec davantage de pays.

Lundi 16 novembre, les ministres des Affaires étrangères de l'UE discutent du renforcement de l'aide à l'Ukraine avant l'hiver, face notamment aux frappes russes contre ses infrastructures. Ils examineront aussi la situation en Syrie et au Proche-Orient.

Du lundi 16 au mercredi 18 novembre, une conférence internationale sur le déminage en Ukraine se tient à Bruxelles. L'objectif est de mobiliser des financements et du matériel pour retirer les mines et explosifs qui empêchent le retour des habitants et la reprise des cultures.

Mardi 17 novembre, la Commission européenne publie ses prévisions économiques d'automne, avec de nouvelles estimations de croissance, d'inflation et de déficits pour les États membres. Des chiffres qui doivent éclairer les débats sur les budgets nationaux, notamment en France.

Mardi 17 novembre, les ministres européens de la Défense discutent de l'aide à la défense aérienne ukrainienne et de la coopération entre fabricants d'armements européens et ukrainiens. Les relations militaires avec les États-Unis et les dépendances envers la Chine figurent également au programme.

Mercredi 18 novembre, le Sénat français vote sur le budget de la Sécurité sociale pour 2027. Le gouvernement souhaite ramener le déficit de 21,8 à 12,7 milliards d'euros, notamment grâce à des économies dans la santé et les retraites.

Jeudi 19 novembre, le Conseil Affaires générales examine la situation de l'état de droit en Hongrie, à Chypre, en Lituanie et au Luxembourg. Les ministres échangeront également sur les priorités législatives de la Commission pour 2027.

Jeudi 19 novembre, les ministres européens de l'Éducation et de la Jeunesse doivent adopter des conclusions sur l'enseignement des sciences et les compétences liées à l'intelligence artificielle. Ils se pencheront aussi sur les moyens d'aider les jeunes à mieux s'informer face aux contenus trompeurs.

Vendredi 20 novembre, de nouvelles règles européennes encadrent les crédits à la consommation, notamment les petits emprunts de moins de 200 euros et certains paiements en trois ou quatre fois proposés lors d'achats en ligne. Les organismes prêteurs devront mieux informer les clients sur le coût total de leur crédit et vérifier leur capacité à rembourser, afin de limiter les risques de surendettement.

Vendredi 20 novembre, l'UE et le Royaume-Uni tiennent un sommet à Bruxelles. Les dirigeants feront le point sur leur coopération en matière de défense et sur les moyens de faciliter les échanges de produits alimentaires depuis le Brexit. Une déclaration commune est attendue à l'issue de la rencontre.

Vendredi 20 novembre, le Sommet européen de l'éducation et des compétences examine comment adapter l'école à l'intelligence artificielle, former les enseignants et lutter contre la baisse du niveau dans les matières fondamentales.

Vendredi 20 novembre, la COP31 sur le climat doit s'achever à Antalya, en Turquie. Les pays tenteront de s'accorder sur l'accélération de la réduction des émissions de gaz à effet de serre. Ils devront également préciser comment tripler d'ici 2035 les financements permettant aux pays les plus vulnérables de faire face aux sécheresses, aux inondations et à la montée des eaux.

Du vendredi 20 au dimanche 22 novembre, des mobilisations coordonnées pour le droit au logement sont annoncées dans sept pays européens : la France, la Belgique, l'Espagne, l'Italie, le Portugal, la Grèce et le Royaume-Uni. Les organisations participantes réclament notamment des mesures contre les loyers trop élevés, les expulsions et la spéculation immobilière.

items.titel: From pin-up calendars to the Istanbul Convention: Magyar’s U-turn, as Operation Purgatory reaches Orbán’s brother (Day 184 of the Tisza government)
items.anriss: The series continues as we report on developments following April’s historic election and on the steps taken since then by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics:

absaetze.t: The series continues as we report on developments following April’s historic election and on the steps taken since then by the Tisza government. This week, we cover the following topics:
Orbán’s brother on a leash
Péter Magyar and women
The new head of state takes on the asset‑protection law
Fidesz is in freefall – no one knows where it will stop
Even Fidesz voters consider uncovering corruption cases important
Áron Orbán on a leash

For 16 years it had been utterly unthinkable that an official measure could reach all the way into former prime minister Viktor Orbán’s family. Now this has happened. On Monday (9 November), Áron Orbán, the brother of the former prime minister, was taken into custody. And not only was he detained, he was later also remanded in pre‑trial detention for one month due to the risk of tampering with evidence.

Áron Orbán’s case, which has been taken over by the National Office for Asset Recovery and Asset Protection set up by the new government, is rather convoluted. Put simply, it concerns a group which, citing its political connections, told companies and entrepreneurs engaged in recruiting foreign labour that if they arranged residence permits through them, they would in any case obtain the necessary visas.

In the case, an investigation was launched on suspicion of influence peddling and other criminal offences, but it did not move forward until the elections; afterwards, however, several arrests were made.

This offers an intriguing parallel with current events in Serbia: there, the authorities set about the dirty work almost immediately after former president Aleksandar Vučić’s fall and arrested major players – clearly everything had long been prepared there as well, only those in power had not allowed the wheels of justice to turn.
According to the Budapest Prosecutor’s Office, over several months in 2024 Áron Orbán and his three associates helped Vietnamese citizens get to Western Europe via Hungary.

According to the allegations, they assisted in visa procedures at Hungarian consular posts, for which they charged a so‑called recruitment fee per person and then shared the proceeds. Based on the authorities’ information, they may have helped more than one hundred Vietnamese nationals.
At the start of the week, it looked like prime minister Péter Magyar was heading for a difficult week in office.

On Monday, he addressed parliament about his government’s first six months, but attention quickly shifted to a controversy over communist-era secret police records. Lists published from the archives wrongly identified 164 people, including Fidesz politician Sándor Lezsák, as former agents, when they had actually been victims of surveillance.

Magyar apologised but argued that the archives are controlled by parliament, not his government. However, since making these records public was a long-promised part of his political agenda, he should take responsibility for the mistake rather than shift the blame.

On top of that, Magyar also bungled the latest episode of his ongoing political communication soap opera, called Absolute Movie Theater. On Sunday, in his video he showed viewers the lesser‑known parts of the Parliament building, where calendars featuring naked women could be seen on the wall of a basement maintenance workshop.

Our former colleague Veronika Munk, editor‑in‑chief of 444.hu, directly confronted the issue in an opinion piece, sharply criticising the video, the objectification of women’s bodies and the conspiratorial, primitive machismo.

The Hungarian prime minister, a prolific Facebook commenter, could not resist weighing in. Commenting under the 444 article, he mocked Munk’s view that crude, breast-focused images are among the most degrading ways women are portrayed in the media. Clearly, he did not agree.

The situation was further aggravated by the fact that on Wednesday the parliamentary committee investigating abuses in the enforcement system under the previous regime – the Völner–Schadl case – heard Judit Varga, Péter Magyar’s ex‑wife and Viktor Orbán’s former justice minister.

The former minister did not say much that was new about the case itself, stating that she had had no opportunity to “expose” her former state secretary, Pál Völner, who was up to his neck in the affair. She spoke much more, however, about her ex‑husband, even though this was not really relevant to the subject.

But Magyar’s superpower is that he can always turn things around. And on Thursday morning (12 November), he did just that. In a video he announced that, after many months of work, a comprehensive social and criminal‑law package would be adopted to protect victims of domestic violence and abused women.
According to Magyar’s announcement, the package contains a large number of very important commitments.
They would tighten restraining‑order rules, so that after a request for help the abuser could not approach the victim, for example, at her home or workplace.
They would make the misuse of intimate recordings a standalone criminal offence.
They would clearly enshrine the requirement of voluntary consent for sexual acts.
They would ensure special treatment for victims of relationship violence in criminal proceedings.

They would amend the heartbeat decree. Before terminating a pregnancy, after receiving medical information, the woman concerned could decide for herself whether she wants the signs of the foetus’s vital functions to be shown to her.
They would abolish the prescription requirement for the morning‑after pill, so emergency contraception would be available without a prescription.
They would launch measures against period poverty, so that those for whom buying basic hygiene products is a financial burden can also obtain them.
They would strengthen support for pregnant women.

The government will initiate the ratification of the Istanbul Convention. The convention lays down obligations for preventing violence against women and domestic violence, protecting victims and prosecuting perpetrators.
Neither the amendment of the heartbeat decree nor the ratification of the Istanbul Convention featured in Tisza’s election programme.
The new head of state is not a signing machine

Hungary’s new president, András Baka, has shown that he will not automatically approve everything put before him. This week, he refused to sign a government-backed law that could give the state greater influence over investment funds and weaken protections for minority shareholders.

Baka argued that the law was too broad, could affect existing funds with no state involvement, and offered insufficient protection to smaller investors. He also criticised the fact that it was passed just 26 hours after being introduced, without proper consultation, warning that such unpredictable interventions could undermine investor confidence. He has referred the legislation to the Constitutional Court for review.

His decision marks a significant departure from the practice of his predecessors, who rarely challenged laws important to the government. For the first time in years, Hungary has a president willing to use his office to question legislation on substantive grounds – a welcome sign for the country's democracy.

Meanwhile, former PM Viktor Orbán and his circle are still not in very good shape. Medián, the polling agency that predicted the election results most accurately, published a new survey at the beginning of the week, according to which Fidesz’s support has plummeted – while Tisza’s has risen.

The voters clearly do not feel that “Tisza‑style despotism” is raging, as Fidesz politicians keep repeating like a mantra. In the total population, 55 percent would currently vote for the governing party, while Fidesz has fallen to 16 percent. This is a low not seen for several decades; they were last this weak in the mid‑1990s.

With such a vote share, Tisza would win more than 160 seats in parliament if elections were held now. And misfortune is piling up for Fidesz: its more uncertain voters are likely drifting into the camp of non‑voters or to Tisza, while its core electorate and more radical base appear to be eroded by the far‑right Mi Hazánk party.

So the tables have turned on what Fidesz itself did with the far right for 16 years – it took over its themes, slowly absorbed its voters and turned this kind of political aggression into the mainstream. Now, everything is slowly returning to the “normal order of things”.

Another survey by Medián has produced data that will make Fidesz scratch its head even more. The poll, commissioned by newspaper HVG, shows that four‑fifths of Hungarians consider it important to uncover corruption cases from the past 16 years and hold perpetrators to account – and only eight percent see this as of little importance.

From the results it is easy to infer why Orbán’s “martyr‑making” strategy is not working. A majority is satisfied with the accountability process itself – 57 percent of people are satisfied with how criminal proceedings have been launched. True, two‑thirds of Fidesz voters think the process is heading in the wrong direction, but even so, eight percent of them believe the proceedings are fine.
Operation Purgatory is in fact criticised from two directions: one‑fifth of people think the pace is not fast and firm enough. Another fifth, by contrast, think the process is too harsh.

What is clear from the numbers is that Fidesz cannot expect much sympathy from undecided voters or supporters of other parties. Least of all from Tisza voters – prayer chains and martyr‑making or not.

And one more detail. Already in May, 65 percent thought that the former prime minister had committed such serious unlawful acts that he should be brought to trial, and the proportion of those who think this has since increased further – even among Fidesz supporters, by four percentage points.

Among Tisza voters, 73 percent believe there is a serious chance this will actually happen, and even one‑third of Fidesz voters consider it likely that Operation Purgatory will reach all the way to Viktor Orbán.

items.titel: US-Unterhändler kündigen Europas Beteiligung bei Ukraine-Verhandlungen an
items.anriss: Von Putin zu Selenskyj - die US-Unterhändler Kushner und Witkoff kommen mit einer Ankündigung aus Moskau nach Dublin. Bei den Verhandlungen sollen künftig auch die Europäer teilnehmen.[ mehr ]

absaetze.t: Friedensgespräche Europa soll mit an den Verhandlungstisch
Von Putin zu Selenskyj - die US-Unterhändler Kushner und Witkoff kommen mit Ankündigungen aus Moskau nach Dublin. Bei den trilateralen Gesprächen sollen auch die Europäer teilhaben.

Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj und der US-Unterhändler Jared Kushner haben eine Beteiligung der Europäer bei Gesprächen über ein Ende des Ukraine-Kriegs in Aussicht gestellt. Er denke, dass Kremlchef Wladimir Putin bereit sei, es zu versuchen, sagte Kushner bei einer Pressekonferenz nach einem Treffen mit Selenskyj in Dublin.

Selenskyj äußerte sich noch deutlicher. Die amerikanische Seite habe Fortschritte gemacht bezüglich der Beteiligung der Europäer an den Gesprächen über ein Ende des Kriegs, sagte Selenskyj. Nächstes Mal werde Europa eine Stimme bei den Verhandlungen haben, sagte er. Außerdem hofft Selenskyj bei den nächsten Friedensgesprächen mit Russland auf Verhandlungen über eine Waffenruhe und eine Deeskalation.

Die beiden US-Unterhändler Steve Witkoff und Jared Kushner hatten sich im Ringen um ein Ende des seit mehr als viereinhalb Jahren andauernden russischen Angriffskriegs zuvor mit Kremlchef Wladimir Putin in Moskau getroffen.
Arbeit an größtem Gefangenenaustausch bisher

Putins außenpolitischer Berater Juri Uschakow äußerte sich nach dem Treffen der US-Unterhändler mit dem Kremlchef noch verhalten zu einer europäischen Beteiligung. "Sie bemühen sich, auf jede Art und Weise an den Verhandlungen teilzunehmen, aber, wie unser Präsident gesagt hat, müssen sie klären, ob sie Frieden wollen oder eine Fortsetzung des Kriegs."

Später erklärte US-Sondergesandter Kushner, die USA arbeite an dem bislang größten Gefangenenaustausch im Krieg zwischen Russland und der Ukraine. Der Austausch werde möglicherweise Tausende Menschen wieder mit ihren Familien zusammenbringen, teilte er auf der Kurznachrichtenplattform X mit. Moskau und Kiew hätten sich zudem darauf geeinigt, die nächste Verhandlungsrunde auf europäische Staaten auszuweiten.

Diese Gespräche folgten auf Verhandlungen am Dienstag und am Mittwoch zwischen Vertretern aus Moskau und Kiew unter US-Vermittlung in Abu Dhabi. Es waren die ersten direkten Gespräche der Kriegsparteien unter US-Vermittlung seit mehr als acht Monaten. Als einzig greifbares Ergebnis wurde ein weiterer, großer Gefangenenaustausch angekündigt.

items.titel: Yemen’s Houthis renew strikes on Saudi Arabia as UNSC extends sanctions
items.anriss: Saudi-led coalition intercepts flurry of suspected Houthi drones targeting oil and military infrastructure.

absaetze.t: Saudi-led coalition intercepts flurry of suspected Houthi missiles, drones targeting oil, military infrastructure.

Saudi-led coalition forces have said they intercepted suspected Houthi drones over Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh region and Eastern Province, as the UN Security Council agreed to extend sanctions on the Iran-allied group.
Major General Turki al-Maliki, the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, announced the interceptions of suspected Houthi drones on Thursday, in a statement carried by the Saudi Press Agency.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had targeted oil infrastructure and military assets in the kingdom, including a pumping station on the East-West Pipeline with a drone as well as the Yanbu oil facility on the Red Sea.
Riyadh says it has rerouted about 4 million barrels of crude per day via its East-West Pipeline to Yanbu, equivalent to about 4 percent of global supply.

Saree further claimed a military cargo plane at Sharurah airport close to Yemen’s border was targeted with a drone, while a ballistic missile launched towards Khamis Mushait airbase “scored a direct hit”.

The Houthi spokesperson added that their forces had targeted the Saudi Aramco headquarters in the capital, Riyadh, but rejected as a “grave falsehood” a Saudi assertion that the group had targeted the kingdom’s Mecca region on Wednesday.

Saudi-backed coalition forces fighting on behalf of Yemen’s internationally recognised government say they continue to confront the Houthis across all frontlines, targeting leaders, vehicles, reinforcements, weapons and positions.

Yemen’s Defence Ministry, citing the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, said the battle against the Houthis was moving towards its “desired objectives”, according to Yemen’s official pro-government Saba news agency.

A meeting convened by the Defence Ministry was held in the Marib governorate to discuss the ongoing operations against the Houthis, where ways to enhance coordination and integration between various military units that are part of the Dawn of Yemen offensive were also discussed.
Security Council extends sanctions

On Thursday, the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) unanimously voted in favour of extending sanctions related to Yemen for one more year, including freezing assets and enforcing travel bans, while demanding an end to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The mandate for the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen, which made the recommendations, was also extended.

UNSC members called on “all parties to refrain from escalatory actions and to resolve differences and disputes through negotiation”, while also backing the territorial integrity of both Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

“The resolution condemns the military escalation by the Houthis, their maritime and cross-border attacks against Saudi Arabia, and their threats to commercial shipping vessels,” the UNSC statement said.

The resolution emphasised that measures taken for the purpose of maintaining sanctions “shall not apply to humanitarian assistance or supplies for basic needs of civilians, without negatively affecting legitimate trade activities”.
“The council sanctions are merely a means, not an end in themselves,” said Ambassador Fu Cong, China’s envoy to the UN, who hoped that “the situation in Yemen will de-escalate as soon as possible”.
333,000 displaced

On Thursday, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said more than 333,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since the beginning of August, including more than 24,000 displaced in the past week.
Civilians “continue to pay a heavy price as violence damages health facilities, forces families from their homes, and hinders the work of humanitarians”, OCHA said.

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is pressing the European Union to adopt an EU Parliament resolution to designate the Ansar Allah Houthi movement as a “terrorist organisation”, according to the Reuters news agency, citing sources familiar with the drive.
But European officials told Reuters the bloc is concerned this could undermine a future peace process.

EU foreign policy spokesperson Anouar El-Anouni said the bloc was in regular contact with Riyadh on regional developments, but declined to comment on any specific discussions under way, according to Reuters.

items.titel: Russian court jails rights lawyer for 12 years on treason charge
items.anriss: Prosecutors say the woman shared security details with Ukraine, while her lawyers argue the information was not secret.

absaetze.t: Prosecutors say the woman shared security details with Ukraine, while her lawyers argue the information wasn’t secret.

A court in Russia’s Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad has sentenced a 66-year-old rights lawyer to 12 years in prison for treason, after prosecutors accused her of passing sensitive information to Ukraine.

The court imposed the sentence on Thursday on Maria Bontsler, according to the rights group Slovo Zashchite, which said she had worked with a number of defendants accused of political offences in Kaliningrad.
The territory sits on the Baltic Sea between Lithuania and Poland.

A court statement posted on Telegram did not name her, but said she had been detained by the FSB intelligence agency on allegations of passing information to Ukraine beginning in 2024 about security officers in Kaliningrad.
Prosecutors also alleged she gave Ukraine information on criminal cases in the exclave that were of interest to Kyiv, the statement said.
She was also given an extra year of restrictions on her activity. Prosecutors had sought 15 years, according to Slovo Zashchite.
Closed trial

Slovo Zashchite said the trial was held behind closed doors, with Bontsler and her lawyers prevented from attending, and that she was allowed only to make a closing statement. It said her lawyers argued that none of the information cited by prosecutors was secret, and that she had been in ill health in detention.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, parliament has approved laws that make public actions aimed at “discrediting” the army illegal and ban the spread of “fake news” about the armed forces.

Russian courts have also jailed lawyers who took on politically sensitive cases. In January 2025, a court sentenced three lawyers of the late opposition leader Alexey Navalny to between three and a half and five and a half years on “extremism” charges, in a case widely seen as an effort to discourage defence lawyers from taking political cases.

items.titel: US: New Congress members pose for traditional photo at Capitol
items.anriss: Newly elected US lawmakers gathered on Capitol Hill on Thursday 12 November for a traditional group photograph ahead of the opening of the 120th Congress. The incoming House members are attending orientation following the November midterm …

absaetze.t: Footage captures newly elected members of the US House of Representatives ascending the Capitol steps, mingling in clusters and exchanging warm greetings, some punctuated by enthusiastic high-fives. Drawn from Illinois, Iowa, Michigan, New York, Virginia and beyond, the freshman cohort gathered for a mandatory orientation programme designed to introduce first-time lawmakers to parliamentary protocol, their impending duties and life on Capitol Hill.
ADVERTISEMENT

Their arrival in Washington follows November’s midterm elections, which yielded sweeping gains for the Democrats alongside a markedly smaller intake of Republicans. This transitional phase sees incoming politicians crossing paths with departing incumbents clearing their desks, signalling the formal handover to the next legislature.

Over the coming weeks, novices will immerse themselves in legislative mechanics and institutional operations before the 120th Congress convenes on 3 January 2027, when members will take the oath of office and formally assume their mandates.

items.titel: The Air Force’s Newest Trainer Is An Aerial Stunt Plane
items.anriss: The U.S. Air Force unveiled its newest aircraft today by flying them over the Air Force Academy , where they will be used to train a future generation of pilots and serve as the basis for a new aerial demonstration team. The goal is to …

absaetze.t: The U.S. Air Force unveiled its newest aircraft today by flying them over the Air Force Academy, where they will be used to train a future generation of pilots and serve as the basis for a new aerial demonstration team. The goal is to give cadets a chance to experience high g-force flying while also providing a new recruiting tool to boost the flagging ranks of Air Force pilots.

Dubbed the T-19A Kestrel, the aircraft are two-seat, single-engine GB1 Gamebird all-carbon-fiber aerial performance planes. They were made by Game Aerospace Composites, a Bentonville, Arkansas, company that describes these planes as “the ultimate aerobatic aircraft for pilots seeking an exhilarating flying experience.”
The Air Force has received four of these planes.
A Boost For Pilot Training

The flight over the Cadet Wing’s noon meal formation “marks the formal arrival of the Academy’s first powered aerobatic aircraft, which recently completed its final military certification flights,” the Air Force noted in a release Thursday afternoon.

The T-19As “will enhance the Academy’s elite airmanship program,” the Air Force added. “By partnering with world-class civilian aerobatic pilots and curriculum developers, the Academy aims to field a nationally competitive aerobatic and demonstration team.”
The Air Force’s top general called the T-19A program “historic.”

“Going from an idea to four aircraft built and delivered in 10 months is unprecedented and a testament to the vision, dedication, and teamwork of everyone who made this possible,” said Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach. “These aircraft will give cadets an opportunity to further develop their airmanship and will ultimately establish a competitive flying team to inspire future Airmen.”
The T-19A “enables cadets to build more flight time and aerobatic aviation experience prior to entering the Air Force or Undergraduate Pilot Training,” the general added.

“From inception to delivery, these aircraft reflect the speed and innovation that strengthens the Department of the Air Force,” said Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink. “As the Kestrel program matures at USAFA, cadets will eventually take on a greater role in training and demonstrations — better preparing them for active-duty pilot training after graduation.”
The program’s long-term goal is to “build a premier capability that evolves to include greater cadet involvement in training, demonstrations and program operations,” the Air Force further explained.
You can see this type of aircraft in action in the following video of GB1 Gamebirds flying and being built.
Unique Procurement Path

Unlike other new aircraft the Air Force has fielded, such as the T-7A Red Hawk jet trainer, the T-19As did not require a lengthy, expensive development and procurement process. They were delivered in under a year and paid for through “a gift from corporate and civilian donations and the Air Force,” an Air Force official told us.

“The acquisition of the four T-19A aircraft was made possible entirely through these donations, requiring no initial procurement funding from the Air Force,” the official added. “The gift is worth $3 million.”

The Air Force “invested approximately $400,000 to supplement the gift of initial spares, and the procurement of necessary support equipment and aircrew flight equipment for the initial cadre and future cadets,” the official noted.

Funding for operations and maintenance “will be programmed through standard Air Force budget processes,” the official explained. “The annual amount to sustain the aircraft is just over $1 million and will be funded through the weapon system sustainment accounts. The annual costs will cover operations and support to manage/sustain the T-19A fleet, and temporary duty travel to national collegiate aerobatic competitions.”
A Flying Recruitment Tool

“The arrival of the T-19A marks an exciting new chapter in airmanship training here at the Academy,” said Lt. Gen. Paul D. Moga, Academy superintendent. “This aircraft will provide an opportunity to train our cadets in ways that were previously not possible. We will strengthen their aviation skills and develop the confidence, discipline and leadership required of future Air Force officers.”

The T-19A is fully cleared for Academy operations, Moga added. The superintendent “selected six active-duty military pilots from the Academy staff and its 306th Flying Training Group to serve as the initial cadre responsible for developing and executing an aerobatic training curriculum,” according to the service. “They will methodically and deliberately integrate the aircraft into the institution’s airmanship program, ultimately establishing a national demonstration and competition team.”

Initially, the active-duty pilots will serve as the primary pilots for the demonstration team, where they will perform at “high-profile recruiting events and air shows nationwide,” the service stated. “In the future, the team will manage a competitive division, participating in International Aerobatic Club and equivalent competitions.”
As noted earlier in this story, all this is taking place as the Air Force is having a hard time finding and keeping pilots.

In Fiscal Year 2024, “the then-Vice Chief of Staff of the Air Force General James C. Slife stated that USAF was 1,900 pilots short of the 19,136 pilots that the service identified as needed for global requirements,” according to a Congressional Research Service (CRS) report released in September. “USAF has a goal of producing approximately 1,500 pilots annually through the Undergraduate Pilot Training program. A House Armed Services Committee report (H.Rept. 119-231) accompanying the committee-reported version of an FY2026 NDAA (H.R. 3838) noted that the service had not met the target.”
What’s In A Name?
The T-19A earned the Kestrel moniker thanks to a group of cadets who came together to recommend the name.

They chose it “because kestrels are falcons known for their agility, acceleration, razor-sharp vision and ability to strike with precision — all traits the aircraft will bring to the Academy’s flight programs,” the Air Force touted.

All T-19A operations will be based out of the U.S. Air Force Academy’s Davis Airfield. “Because safety is the foundational block of the program, operations will utilize a robust Safety Management System tailored specifically for low-altitude, high-performance aerobatics,” according to the Air Force. “All flight and ground operations will follow the more restrictive requirements of Federal Aviation Administration regulations and/or U.S. Air Force safety instructions.”

We asked the Air Force when the cadets will begin training and when the new Kestrel demonstration team will start flying. There are plenty of folks at the Academy waiting to find out the answers to both of those questions.

items.titel: High-Speed Aircraft Startup Hermeus Joins Forces With Northrop Grumman
items.anriss: Aviation startup Hermeus and established prime contractor Northrop Grumman say they are now working together toward the aim of delivering operational uncrewed aircraft capable of high-supersonic, if not hypersonic , flight to the U.S. …

absaetze.t: Aviation startup Hermeus and established prime contractor Northrop Grumman say they are now working together toward the aim of delivering operational uncrewed aircraft capable of high-supersonic, if not hypersonic, flight to the U.S. military. Through a newly announced partnership, Northrop Grumman is set to integrate electronic warfare systems, sensors, autonomy packages, and other capabilities onto “next-generation” Hermeus drones.

Hermeus and Northrop Grumman announced their team-up earlier today. Hermeus, which was founded in 2018, has already flown a succession of ever-more capable uncrewed jet-powered Quarterhorse demonstrator drones. The delta-winged Quarterhorse Mk 2.1 was the first of these to break the sound barrier during a test flight in May. The company is now working on a further evolved Quarterhorse Mk 2.2, which it hopes to push beyond Mach 2.

Hermeus’ stated end goal is a design capable of hypersonic flight. The company has also previously shown renderings of a planned “mission plane” prototype described as being capable of “high-Mach” flight and equipped with six underwing pylons, three under each wing, as well as one along the centerline.

Quarterhorse Mk 2.1 has already demonstrated the ability to release stores at high speed. In September, Hermeus also unveiled Ramjet-X, a smaller ramjet-powered platform that can be air-launched from Quarterhorse drones, ostensibly to support high-speed flight testing activities, but that could be adapted to operational missions.

Now, as part of the new partnership, “Northrop Grumman will provide integrated mission systems design, development, integration, and sustainment for Hermeus’ next-generation aircraft — reusable, unmanned high-Mach platforms designed to deliver affordable capability on relevant timelines,” according to a press release from Hermeus. “The collaboration creates a path to equip Hermeus’ aircraft with technology across sensing, communications, navigation, and command and control, allowing the aircraft to operate more intelligently and take on more complex missions” and “give warfighters faster, more survivable options in combat.”

“As the threat environment accelerates, the Department of War needs autonomous systems developed and fielded in months, not years,” per a separate Northrop Grumman press release. “Northrop Grumman and Hermeus will meet that need by pairing Northrop Grumman’s combat‑proven mission systems and ‘ready‑now’ electronic warfare, communication, sensing and autonomy expertise with Hermeus’ high‑speed Quarterhorse aircraft.”

“We’re building a new class of aircraft that gives the warfighter improved speed, range, and flexibility while integrating into the existing Force,” Zach Shore, CEO of Hermeus, also said in a statement. “Adding Northrop Grumman’s battle-tested mission systems will push what those aircraft can do in real world scenarios and help us field operational capability faster. Northrop brings decades of experience turning aircraft into effective mission platforms and that’s exactly what we want to tap into.”

Beyond the mention of electronic warfare, sensing, and communications capabilities, neither company’s press release elaborates more specifically on the kind of operational missions that future Hermeus drones could be tasked with. It is also unclear which branches of the U.S. military might be looking to fly them. TWZ has reached out for more information.

That being said, development of the Quarterhorse family has been supported in part through contracts from the U.S. Air Force and the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU). The aforementioned stores release testing was conducted under the auspices of a DIU effort called High-Cadence Airborne Testing Capabilities (HyCAT).

Hermeus’ inclusion in HyCAT brought “a technical focus on turbine-based combined cycle [TBCC] propulsion and a pathway for dual-use, reusable hypersonic flight aircraft,” according to a DIU press release back in 2023. “Hermeus will emphasize demonstration of enabling technologies – aircraft sub-systems and mission integration – needed for future hypersonic aircraft.”
Hermeus has also been developing a TBCC propulsion system called Chimera. The company’s goal is to integrate that onto a future Quarterhorse Mk 3 design.
As we have written previously:

“A practical TBCC propulsion system has long been viewed as something of a holy grail for very high-speed aircraft design. Ramjets and scramjets typically used to propel air-breathing air vehicles to hypersonic speeds, typically defined as anything above Mach 5, do not work properly at subsonic speeds and can have trouble operating efficiently even at low-supersonic speeds. As such, a significant initial boost velocity, usually provided by a rocket motor, is required before those engines can kick in. A TBCC combines ramjets/scramjets with jet turbines that work at lower speeds and offers the ability to seamlessly shift from one mode to the other. An air vehicle with a TBCC propulsion system would be able to take off and land from suitably long existing runways, but cruise at high-supersonic or even hypersonic speeds, offering immense operational flexibility.”

Furthermore, the U.S. Air Force has been open in recent years about at least having an interest in reusable hypersonic air vehicles capable of performing strike and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) missions. The service has publicly pursued the development of relevant technologies, including advanced scramjet engines and TBCC propulsion concepts, and full-up demonstrators to prove them out, through several programs in recent years, but the outcomes to date remain unclear.

The Air Force did award Leidos a contract for the development of a full-up prototype reusable hypersonic air vehicle under its secretive Mayhem program back in 2022. That effort, which aimed to demonstrate a platform that could be adapted to hypersonic strike and ISR missions, ran into budget and other hurdles, and its status was decidedly murky as of 2024. That same year, a very similar-sounding project called Next Generation Responsive Strike (Next RS) emerged at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA), in which the Air Force was also involved. As of 2025, the Next RS plan also included plans to acquire a flying prototype or demonstrator by 2030, but how that effort has advanced since then is unclear.
As we have also written in the past:

“A reusable uncrewed air-launched hypersonic strike and reconnaissance aircraft could certainly offer benefits in various operational scenarios. Such a system could be ideal for prosecuting time-sensitive targets, or just gathering intelligence on them, including deep in denied areas at extreme stand-off ranges. From an ISR perspective, spy satellites, which might be the only other option for collecting on the targets in question, could take too long to retask and are predictable, with the enemy knowing when they will pass overhead.”
“An air-launched reusable platform could offer additional flexibility in terms of vector of approach and timely arrival over a target area compared to regional ground and surface-launched concepts.”

Northrop Grumman’s press release today highlights the potential to add electronic warfare capabilities to the mix. It’s not clear whether the aim here is to provide self-production for the drone or to enable non-kinetic attacks, or both. An electronic warfare package could also allow the vehicle to act as a very-high-speed reusable decoy.

It’s also important to note that a design from Hermeus would not need to be capable of hypersonic flight, defined as anything above Mach 5, to be relevant in the roles described above. As mentioned earlier, even before today’s announcement, the company had plans for an operationalized ‘high-Mach’ drone. We have also already seen such capability fielded in China in the form of the WZ-8, a rocket-powered tactical theater reconnaissance drone.

Aircraft, crewed and uncrewed, that can fly at transitional speeds between the high-supersonic and fully hypersonic regimes are also set to be increasingly relevant for research and development and test and evaluation activities. This is the arena where Hermeus is working now through efforts like HyCAT. Growing demand for these kinds of high-speed flight test capabilities has also recently been underscored by reports that NASA is exploring returning a retired SR-71 Blackbird to flight as an experimental X-plane.

There is clearly work still to be done before any version of Quarterhorse, or a future design from Hermeus, emerges as an operational platform, hypersonic or not. At the same time, the new partnership with Northrop Grumman reflects a new and very explicit step toward that goal, which is building on work already being done with the support of the U.S. military.

items.titel: Protesters Urge Steven Spielberg to Boycott MoMA Over Leon Black’s Epstein Ties
items.anriss: Ahead of the Museum of Modern Art's (MoMA) annual benefit for its Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center tonight, November 12, about 20 protesters assembled outside the institution to call on the gala's honoree, Steven Spielberg, to …

absaetze.t: Activists rallied at the museum ahead of a benefit for the Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center, decrying the board member’s Epstein connections and his pro-Israel support.
November 12, 2026 — 4 min read

Ahead of the Museum of Modern Art's (MoMA) annual benefit for its Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center tonight, November 12, about 20 protesters assembled outside the institution to call on the gala's honoree, Steven Spielberg, to reject the recognition. The protest comes amid growing calls to oust Leon Black from the museum board over his ties to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A letter sent to Spielberg by the feminist campaign group We Are UltraViolet, reviewed by Hyperallergic, urges the Academy Award-winning director to boycott MoMA until the institution severs ties with Black and renames the film venue.

“MoMA has benefited so handsomely from Black that they have named the very room you will be honored in, the Debra and Leon Black Family Film Center, in his honor,” reads the missive to Spielberg, authored by Elisa Batista, campaign director of UltraViolet. For the past four iterations of the benefit, MoMA has funneled all proceeds into the film center, which was created in 2019 in recognition of a $40 million gift from the private equity tycoon.
“Mr. Spielberg, you do NOT want your legacy connected to accused abuser and Epstein associate Leon Black,” Bautista continues.

The letter makes reference to three sexual assault and misconduct accusations brought forth against the billionaire, all of which Black denies. One of the lawsuits was discontinued by the plaintiff, and an earlier lawsuit was dismissed by the court. A third lawsuit was allowed to move forward after a judge imposed a sanction. UltraViolet said it has not received a response from Spielberg's representatives.

Black left his role as CEO of his private equity firm Apollo Global Management in 2021, when news broke that he paid Epstein $158 million for financial advice from 2012 to 2017, after Epstein’s first conviction for soliciting sex from a minor. Even though he stepped down as MoMA board chairman that same year, after Hyperallergic published an open letter signed by over 150 artists calling for his removal, Black remains a MoMA board trustee.

Public scrutiny of Black intensified in September, after the US House of Representatives unanimously approved a resolution to hold the MoMA trustee in contempt of Congress for defying subpoenas in an Epstein investigation. This month, Black sued California Representative Robert Garcia for defamation over public comments such as "Leon Black is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”
Playwright and theater artist Gracie Gardner, who initially posted an open letter to Spielberg on her Instagram, said she was “amazed” by the public response.

“Steven Spielberg has made his career making stories about the dignity of women and children,” Gardner told Hyperallergic at tonight's protest. “It's totally disgusting that he's accepting an award [at the film center named after Leon Black], who's currently in contempt of Congress for not producing NDAs and his involvement in the Epstein files.”
Last month, Gardner co-performed a staged reading of former Barclays CEO and JP Morgan executive Jes Staley's deposition on Epstein to the United States House Oversight Committee in July.

At this evening's protest, others carried signs pointing to Black's connections to pro-Israel and Zionist organizations. Black has reportedly donated money to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which denies that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, and Birthright Israel, which is accused of serving as a propaganda campaign for the Israeli government.

“I can personally say I'm Jewish and it's specifically because of my Jewish values that we're here. Never again means never again for anyone,” one demonstrator, Janet Goodman-Clarke, told Hyperallergic. “Leon Black not only is a Zionist, but he's also named ad nauseam in the Epstein files.”
MoMA has not replied to Hyperallergic's request for comment.

Artists, activists, and Epstein survivors have repeatedly gathered in front of MoMA demanding his ousting. Among those in attendance at today's action was Katie Fuller, arts educator and founder of the Time and Memory Project, who staged a separate protest calling for Black's removal in front of the museum with her sister in September.

Last month, Fuller teamed up with Epstein survivors, UltraViolet, and the Epstein-Trump Reading Room, created by the Institute for Primary Facts, to illustrate the extent of Epstein's network. The free, mobile installation displayed a timeline of President Donald Trump’s relationship with Epstein and contains thousands of books' worth of the released so-called “Epstein Files,” in which Black was mentioned over 8,500 times.

That protest included Dani Bensky, a dancer, educator, and Epstein survivor from 2004 to 2005. A few weeks after the action, Bensky wrote an op-ed for Hyperallergic condemning Black’s board position as “one of the starkest examples of institutional ignorance — a head-in-the-sand, look-the-other-way mentality that will inevitably give abuse of power a dark corner to grow and fester in.”

Besides his investments in MoMA, Black has held enormous sway in the art world. In a newly released book by William D. Cohan, Black disclosed plans to convert the Woolworth Mansion into a tax-beneficial art foundation, which is expected to house works from his estimated $5 billion art collection, an asset that Epstein helped leverage as bank collateral.

Gardner said she had one simple message for the attendees of tonight’s benefit gala: “If you know, you're human garbage. And if you didn't know, you can't say that after tonight, because we're out here saying hi to everybody with our signs.”

items.titel: By looking at the world through a US lens, the West overestimates China’s resolve to invade Taiwan
items.anriss: Whenever there’s a destabilising event in the West, foreign-policy discussions inevitably turn to the China-Taiwan question. Will Xi Jinping use the event as an opportunity to invade his country’s island neighbour? The humbling of Donald …

absaetze.t: Affairs
November 13, 2026
4 Min Read
The West’s perception of Asia is clouded by the US’s approach towards foreign policy. But while Donald Trump tends towards unprovoked invasions, Xi Jinping’s priorities lie beyond invading Taiwan.

Whenever there’s a destabilising event in the West, foreign-policy discussions inevitably turn to the China-Taiwan question. Will Xi Jinping use the event as an opportunity to invade his country’s island neighbour? The humbling of Donald Trump’s Republican Party after last week’s US midterm elections is the latest example of this rote formula. Endlessly linking what happens in Washington to Beijing speaks more about US hubris and than an understanding of how China operates. The unhelpful conjecture has to stop.

No one outside Zhongnanhai – China’s leadership compound in Beijing – knows what Xi Jinping is thinking. The best that we can do is guess. My estimate is that he wasn’t hosting a US election watch party, eagerly awaiting the results so that he could call up his generals and go over the latest invasion plans. There’s no denying that Beijing wants Taiwan back in the fold and that the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) will almost certainly invade if provoked. Xi won’t, however, be so overtly opportunistic.

The president will try to avoid war against a country that he views as a part of mainland China, only pursuing a military option when success is certain. And even then – without going all Sun Tzu’s The Art of War – success does not mean an initial victory on the battlefield. We only need to look at George W Bush’s infamous 2003 “Mission Accomplished” speech, delivered some two months after the US-led coalition invaded Iraq and more than 23 years before the last American troops withdrew.

Beijing has time on its side and Zhongnanhai has far more patience than the White House. Mao Zedong was said to have told Henry Kissinger in the 1970s that the country could wait 100 years to resolve the Taiwan question. So, at the earliest, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP)’s countdown clock ends in 2049, when it aims to complete its “Chinese Dream” of national rejuvenation.

The ideal scenario for China would be for Taiwan to opt for reunification but this dream grows ever more fanciful with every generation. An end to the island’s independence is more likely to happen only when it has no other choice: either if Washington’s security promises falter or if the PLA becomes demonstrably stronger than the US Army.

Xi’s legacy project is ultimately to cement CCP rule in China rather than capture Taiwan. This requires restoring China to what the party sees as its rightful place as the richest, strongest and most respected country in the region, while overcoming domestic obstacles, from a stubborn housing crisis to high youth unemployment. For all the talk about China becoming more “assertive” and “belligerent” towards Taiwan, only its techniques and technology are new. The country’s mission and behaviour can be seen as the mere continuation of a project to restore wounded pride.

The fundamental trap that the West keeps falling into is judging China by US standards rather than by its own track record. Thirteen years into Xi’s presidency, China’s standing is sky high and Beijing is winning on many fronts, including technology, defence and soft-power exports such as brands and entertainment. The nation is winning hearts and minds across Asia and Global Majority countries, while a tattered Uncle Sam splashes around in the gutter, exporting hate and rattling the global economy. China’s reputation should continue to rise, provided that Beijing doesn’t do anything to compromise Asia’s current stability.

We have to remember that, while superpowers might throw their weight around, they don’t necessarily all have the same playbook. Creating idiotic acronyms such as Crink is lazy and demonstrates the West’s inability to acknowledge what the US has been up to all this time. America and Russia are the only two major powers that have invaded other sovereign nations unprovoked this century but there’s no acronym doing the rounds for that duo. Looking ahead, US boots on the ground in Havana in 2027 should have far shorter odds than PLA soldiers in Taipei.

November 12, 2026 — 4 min read
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.
Yukiko Yamagata to Helm NYC's Print Center
New York's Print Center, home to programs and exhibitions celebrating all the art that's pressed, proofed, and published, announced Yukiko Yamagata as its new executive director this week.

Her professional profile doesn't immediately scream “print nerd”: Yamagata most recently served as deputy director at Creative Time and previously worked at the Open Society Foundations, where she led a $15.8 million arts and culture fellowship program for socially engaged artists. But one of her earliest roles in the 1990s was as a senior curatorial assistant in the photo department at the Whitney Museum of American Art, and she is a current board member of Women Photograph, an organization focused on equitable practices in photojournalism and visual media.
Yamagata succeeds Judy Hecker, who announced her decision to step down earlier this year after a decade in the role, and is now executive director emerita.
Natalie Renganeschi to Lead Women's Studio Workshop

The Women's Studio Workshop in Rosendale, New York, dedicated to the printing arts as well as papermaking, bookbinding, photography, and more, has named Natalie Renganeschi as its fourth-ever executive director in the organization's 52-year history.

Renganeschi's career at WSW began in 2018, when she joined as a part-time employee while working as a high school art teacher. Now, she will oversee the nonprofit's major campus expansion, including the relaunch of its ceramics center.

“My path to leadership hasn’t been a traditional one, but it’s rooted in the ethos of WSW,” Renganeschi said in a statement. “Just as our mediums are steeped in process and the history of craft, working here is a sustained act of communal learning that allows for growth to come from below and within.”

items.titel: Philadelphia city council investigates sudden closure of oldest natural history research institution in the Americas
items.anriss: The Academy of Natural Sciences, with a collection of more than 19 million specimens, shuttered in September for financial reasons

absaetze.t: The Academy of Natural Sciences, a 198-year-old public museum in Philadelphia run by Drexel University, shuttered in September because of rising costs. The university’s president will now testify under subpoena before Philadelphia’s city council on 16 November, answering questions about the sudden closure and what will happen to the museum’s valuable collection of more than 19 million specimens.

While many of the Academy’s workers have been laid off, collection managers still on staff have faced an “astronomical increase” in emails and calls, says Amber Redfield, a former geosciences collection manager and fossil preparator at the Academy who was recently laid off and is now volunteering there. She says that people have been asking: “Is this safe?” “Can I see it?” “Can I book an appointment?”

Isa Betancourt, a former curatorial assistant in the entomology department and an organiser with the Save the Academy coalition, says the number of curators has dropped from 11 to five. The invertebrate palaeontology collection manager recently left for a job at the American Museum of Natural History. “There is no plan to replace her," Betancourt tells The Art Newspaper. Endowed curator posts in entomology and palaeontology have gone unfilled for years, she adds.

Founded in 1812, the Academy describes itself as the oldest natural history research institution in the Americas. It opened its museum to the public in 1828 and, in 1868, put Hadrosaurus foulkii on view as the world’s first mounted dinosaur skeleton. Its millions of specimens include plants collected on the Lewis and Clark expedition, John James Audubon’s birds and Thomas Jefferson’s fossils.

The Academy became a Drexel affiliate in 2011, while retaining its status as a separate non-profit with its own board. Drexel recently told the city council it had “stepped in as a partner” that year, when the Academy “faced severe financial distress”.

The city council passed a resolution on 17 September to investigate the Academy’s closing. The resolution calls institutions like the Academy “part of the cultural fabric of the city” and says its shuttering would especially affect area residents “for whom the museum is a fixture of the neighbourhood”. An initial hearing took place on 26 October, which Drexel’s president did not attend.

At the hearing, representatives for Drexel cited the building's "substantial capital needs" and told the city council that public exhibitions need a new model, "almost certainly in a different location".

Sarah McAnulty, a squid biologist and Save the Academy organiser, says city council members asked Drexel representatives to check their numbers. "If all you need to keep the public museum open is a million dollars, what the hell are we doing here?" she says, describing the city council’s reaction.

Staff learned of the Academy’s closure at a morning meeting on 1 September, Redfield says. Most staff were laid off by 1 November, and many people "found out they were let go in a report by The Philadelphia Inquirer", she adds.

Redfield says the museum drew more than 60,000 visitors in its final 12 days of public hours. "That's not enough time to shut down a lifetime of scientific and educational work," she adds. "I planned to retire at the Academy and don't have any backup plans." Now she is volunteering.

"Unfortunately, volunteer labour is essential to most natural history collections, but it’s not sustainable,” Betancourt says. “The fact that the volunteer manager was initially slated for termination and had to be reinstated shows Drexel has no idea how these collections function."

Betancourt adds that the Academy's social media accounts have been inactive for two months and staff do not have access because Drexel controls them. The Academy's director of marketing and communications was let go with the closure. Betancourt says the university may not realise that communications and education staff connect the collections with the public and potential benefactors, "otherwise, the collections work in darkness”.

The William Penn Foundation has offered a year of funding to replace Drexel's subsidy for the museum. "The foundation has not received a response to our offer," a spokesperson told the Inquirer. Drexel later stated that it had not received a "formal proposal with a defined level of financial support".

Betancourt says Save the Academy wants Drexel to explain "why no capital campaign was undertaken" and "why the scientific community has been shut out of behind-the-scenes negotiations. The closed-door negotiations got us a closed museum. Natural history collections tied to a financially haemorrhaging university are not safe natural history collections.”
